story|title:modular workflow governance.content_excerpt: It sits on top of the models and harnesses you already use. It doesn't try to replace them. Status: all seven modules and the control-plane hub ship runnable v0.1 slices with Docker Compose and unit tests. If you've wired up AI tooling for a team, you already know the pieces. LiteLLM or Portkey handle routing. Langfuse, LangSmith or Braintrust handle traces and evals. LangGraph handles orchestration, and OpenMetadata or Atlan handle lineage. Each one is good at its own job. None of them agree on what a project is, which request belongs to which stage, or where the data went after it left the router. So you end up writing glue. You have keys in three places, evals in four dashboards, and a spreadsheet saying which model is allowed to see which data. Mirevox is meant to be that glue, written once, with contracts that travel well enough that you can swap out any of the tools underneath. Apache-2.0. Every module repo and this site ship with Docker Compose and runnable v0.1 slices. Models are at the bottom: Foundry, Bedrock, Vertex, or whatever you run locally. Harnesses sit above them—the workspace around the model, like VS Code with an agent or a chat UI. Mirevox is the layer above the harness. It's the part a non-technical person needs to get work through, and the part an operator needs to see what happened. It isn't another terminal harness. code turnover, PR review tax, AI attribution share, and complexity-adjusted throughput. Most AI tooling stops at the request. Real delivery takes longer than that. Someone has an idea, it turns into requirements, then a design decision, then a spec, then code, then tests. The modules are designed to follow that whole path: high-level requirements, then functional and non-functional requirements, then ADRs, then specs. At each step you get a clear answer to "can I move on yet?" SpecKit or OpenSpec can plug in, but you don't need them. Stages are a metaphor borrowed from ordinary workflows (book a slot, meet the gate, move on)—applied to AI delivery. Advance criteria stay readable; SpecKit and OpenSpec are options, not the only path. Nearly everything here falls into one of two paths. Both can lean on the Context Engine, so each repo gets indexed once and shared, instead of being re-ingested every time an agent starts up. A request comes in from VS Code or the home chatbot, both pointing at the same endpoint. Smart Router decides where it goes—local model or provider—based on the task and what you've said is allowed. story|title:why agent swarms get better.content_excerpt: Vaibhav Kumar / Ibrahim Sheikh / Peter Zhong / Saurav Joshi / Patrick Ma / Jason Dellaluce / Darsh Patel / Phil MacEachron / Michele Catasta · Nov 19, 2026 Fred Brooks observed in 1975 that adding programmers to a late project makes it later because every new engineer brings more coordination than work. Early research on agent swarms found that multi-agent systems often trailed a single agent once coordination costs were accounted for [1–4]. We tested whether this still holds for today’s models using performance engineering tasks to examine how scaling inference-time compute drives both speedups and emergent coordination mechanics. On NumPy, one Claude Opus 5.5 agent made the workloads 3.7× faster in two hours, while a swarm of 32 Opus agents, given the same two hours, reached 18.9×. GPT-6.2 Astra was the strongest solo agent we tested, yet its swarms got worse as they grew. Given no instructions on how to organize, each model’s swarms arranged themselves differently, and the differences mattered. The best swarms sent few direct messages; workers claimed tasks and shared results on a common board. The ones that struggled routed everything through the coordinator, whose inbox grew with every agent added. The other deciding factor was the shape of the work. While codebases with independent problems allowed each new agent to contribute usefully, highly constrained tasks often led extra agents to compete for the same code. On Replit, an agent swarm works much like an engineering team. Each agent, coordinator or worker, is a full Replit Agent with its own cloud sandbox, so it can build, run, and profile code without getting in anyone else’s way. Agents share a repository rather than a filesystem, and their work comes together through branches and pushes. They also share context through three communication channels: a swarm board that lets agents open threads, reply, address posts to specific teammates, and set their status; direct messaging between teammates; and transcripts that let agents read what a teammate tried and why without interrupting it. Agent Habitat provides the elastic compute behind this. Each sandbox is an isolated Linux microVM whose CPU, memory, and disk grow with the workload, so a coordinator can start hundreds of workers quickly, and a single agent can work across several sandboxes at once. story|title:windows run larger local ai.content_excerpt: Many of today's most capable open weight AI models don't fit in a typical PC's memory. When a model is too big for one machine, the usual options are to shrink it, send the work to the cloud, or build a server-class cluster with specialized networking hardware. Today we're announcing a developer preview of RDMA over USB4® on Windows. Connect two or more USB4-capable Windows PCs with USB4 cables, and you can split one model across them, combining their memory and GPU compute. There's no RDMA network adapter to buy, no switch to configure, and no third-party driver to install. It's part of building Windows for hybrid intelligence , where AI work runs on your PC or in the cloud, wherever it fits best. RDMA over USB4 extends what you can run locally, from one PC to a small cluster on your desk. Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) moves data directly between the memory of two systems, bypassing most of the traditional networking stack. That gives low latency and low CPU overhead, which is why RDMA is a staple of datacenter storage and distributed computing. Windows has supported RDMA for years through NetworkDirect , a transport-agnostic RDMA interface, but until now only with dedicated RDMA network adapters for Ethernet and InfiniBand today. Those adapters are built mainly for servers and are rarely found in consumer or developer PCs. Meanwhile, many of today's widely available AI PCs already have USB4® ports, and Windows 11 already supports host-to-host networking over USB4 through its in-box USB4® connection manager. Many Windows PCs already offer USB4-capable connectivity through Thunderbolt™ 4 and Thunderbolt™ 5 ports. Systems meeting the preview requirements can participate. When you split a model across PCs with tensor parallelism, the PCs exchange data many times for every token they generate. At that point latency, more than bandwidth, sets the pace. In our measurements between two PCs, RDMA over USB4® cut round-trip latency for small messages to about 28–50 µs, roughly 4x lower than Ethernet (UDP) over the same USB4 ® link . RDMA brings communication latency down to the same low level at both 40 Gbps and 80 Gbps, while 80 Gbps provides twice the bandwidth. Figure 1. Round-trip latency by message size, RDMA compared with Ethernet over the same USB4® link (lower is better). * For the best performance, use PCs with USB4 ports at 40 Gbps or faster, enough ports to connect every PC directly, and plenty of unified memory, memory bandwidth and GPU compute.
